lesson.title: The Prisoner's Dilemma: A Discount Nobody Wants
lesson.objective: Explain how a choice that pays better for each player individually can leave both players worse off.
lesson.approachReason: One fictional pricing decision lets the learner experience the temptation to compete and then discover its cost to both businesses.

blocks.heading: Two cafés, one decision
blocks.body:
You run Cedar Café, opposite Maple Café, and each café must independently choose tomorrow's price: regular or discount. You choose at the same time, without seeing the other's decision; treat this as a one-day decision with no agreements or future consequences.

For this fictional example, the table gives each café's daily profit after all costs:

| Cedar's choice | Maple's choice | Cedar's profit | Maple's profit |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Regular | Regular | $40 | $40 |
| Discount | Regular | $55 | $15 |
| Regular | Discount | $15 | $55 |
| Discount | Discount | $25 | $25 |

Each owner wants to maximize their own café's profit.
blocks.example: These are invented profits for a simplified game, not a claim about how real café pricing always works.

blocks.heading: Uncertainty doesn't change your best choice
blocks.body:
If Maple chooses regular, discounting gives Cedar $55 rather than $40. If Maple discounts, discounting gives Cedar $25 rather than $15.

So discounting pays Cedar more in either case: you do not need to guess Maple's decision. A choice that gives a higher payoff regardless of the other player's choice is called a strictly dominant strategy.
blocks.example: Compare Cedar's two choices while holding Maple's choice fixed. Comparing $55 with $25 would instead change Maple's choice, so it would not answer which action Cedar should take.

hints: Hold Cedar's choice fixed at discount.
Compare only the two rows where Cedar discounts.
blocks.retry: When Cedar discounts, Maple can choose between $15 from regular pricing and $25 from discounting. The $40 outcome requires Cedar to choose regular too.

blocks.heading: Two sensible decisions, one disappointing result
blocks.body:
Maple faces exactly the same incentives as Cedar: discounting pays more whatever Cedar does. If both owners choose their strictly dominant strategy, both discount and earn $25 each.

Yet both would earn $40 each if both chose regular pricing. This is the prisoner's dilemma: each player's individual incentive pushes toward an outcome that is worse for both than mutual cooperation would be.
blocks.example: In this pricing game, choosing regular plays the role of cooperation, and discounting plays the role of defection. Those labels describe the game's incentives, not the owners' moral character.

blocks.heading: Count the cost to the two cafés
blocks.prompt: Both cafés choose discount and earn $25 each. Both could instead earn $40 each by choosing regular. How much lower is their combined daily profit when both discount?

traps.feedback: That is the loss for one café: 40 − 25 = 15. The question asks for the loss across both cafés.
That is their combined profit when both discount, not the amount lost compared with both choosing regular.

hints: Calculate the combined profit for each of the two outcomes.
Subtract the both-discount total from the both-regular total.
blocks.solution: Both regular: 40 + 40 = 80. Both discount: 25 + 25 = 50. The combined loss is 80 − 50 = 30 dollars.

hints: Start with both cafés choosing regular, then change only Cedar's choice.
Separate what happens to Cedar's profit from what happens to their combined profit.
blocks.retry: A better outcome for both is not necessarily each player's best individual choice. When Maple keeps regular pricing, Cedar can raise its own profit by discounting—even though that cuts Maple's profit.

blocks.heading: Explain the dilemma to your co-owner
blocks.prompt: Your co-owner says, “If both cafés end up worse off, at least one owner must have made a bad calculation.” Write a two-sentence reply using the profits to explain why that conclusion is wrong.
blocks.model: Discounting gives either owner more profit regardless of the other café's choice: $55 instead of $40 against regular, or $25 instead of $15 against discount. Both can therefore calculate correctly for themselves and still end up earning $25 each rather than the $40 each available if both chose regular.

activities.title: Your sealed pricing decision
activities.prompt: You must submit Cedar's pricing decision before learning Maple's choice. Using the profit table, which policy gives you the highest profit in either possible case?
activities.reveal: Discounting wins both comparisons: $55 beats $40 if Maple chooses regular, and $25 beats $15 if Maple discounts. You can identify your best choice without predicting Maple's choice.

options.text: Choose discount regardless of Maple's choice.
options.feedback: You get the higher available profit in either case: $55 against regular or $25 against discount.

options.text: Choose regular regardless of Maple's choice.
options.feedback: You get $40 against regular or $15 against discount. Discounting would give you more in both cases.

options.text: Choose regular if you expect Maple to discount.
options.feedback: Against Maple's discount, regular earns you $15 while discount earns you $25.

options.text: Flip a coin between regular and discount.
options.feedback: The coin sometimes selects regular, which pays less than discount against either of Maple's choices.

questions.question: Maple's owner learns that Cedar will discount. If Maple wants the highest profit for itself, what should it choose?
options: Regular, because Cedar's discount makes Maple's choice irrelevant.
Either price, because both give Maple the same profit.
questions.explanation: With Cedar's discount held fixed, Maple earns $25 by discounting and $15 by choosing regular. Discounting is its better response.

questions.question: The owners notice that both choosing regular would earn them $40 each. Why doesn't recognizing this shared benefit remove the dilemma in this one-day game?
options: Either owner could increase its own profit from $40 to $55 by discounting while the other keeps regular pricing.
Both choosing regular actually produces less combined profit than both discounting.
An owner choosing regular would earn $40 regardless of the other owner's choice.
Discounting is attractive only when an owner expects the other café to choose regular.
questions.correctAnswer: Either owner could increase its own profit from $40 to $55 by discounting while the other keeps regular pricing.
questions.explanation: Both choosing regular is better for both than both discounting, but each owner has an individual incentive to depart from it. Recognizing the shared benefit does not change those payoffs.

problems: The first check's retry mostly repeats the same payoff comparison as its explanation rather than offering a genuinely different explanation.
All tasks use the same cafés and payoff table, so the lesson checks understanding within the example but not whether learners can recognize the dilemma in a new setting.
The combined-profit calculation is accurate but less strategically demanding than the surrounding tasks.
